etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English schadowe, schadewe, schadwe (also schade > shade), from Old English sċeaduwe, sċeadwe, oblique form of sċeadu (“shadow, shade; darkness; protection”), from Proto-West Germanic *skadu, from Proto-Germanic *skadwaz (“shade, shadow”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃- (“darkness”).

definitions.definition: A dark image projected onto a surface where light (or other radiation) is blocked by the shade of an object.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter I, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The stories did not seem to me to touch life.  […]  They left me with the impression of a well-delivered stereopticon lecture, with characters about as life-like as the shadows on the screen, and whisking on and off, at the mercy of the operator.

definitions.definition: Relative darkness, especially as caused by the interruption of light; gloom; obscurity.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto V”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 32:
quote.text: In secret shadow from the sunny ray, / On a sweet bed of lillies softly layd.

quote.citation: 1636 (date written), John Denham, “The Destruction of Troy, an Essay upon the Second Book of Virgils Æneis”, in Poems and Translations, with The Sophy, 4th edition, London:  […]  [John Macock] for H[enry] Herringman […], published 1668, →OCLC:
quote.text: Night's sable shadows from the ocean rise.

definitions.definition: An area protected by an obstacle (likened to an object blocking out sunlight).
(obsolete or poetic) A reflected image, as in a mirror or in water.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ix], page 172, column 2, lines 4–5:
quote.text: Some there be that ſhadowes kiſſe, / Such haue but a ſhadowes bliſſe.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XVI, page 26:
quote.text: […] some dead lakeThat holds the shadow of a lark⁠Hung in the shadow of a heaven […]

quote.citation: 1962, Charles Kinbote [pseudonym; Vladimir Nabokov], Pale Fire, New York, N.Y.: Berkley Books, published November 1985, →ISBN:
quote.text: I was the shadow of the waxwing slainBy the false azure in the windowpane;I was the smudge of ashen fluff—and ILived on, flew on, in the reflected sky.

definitions.definition: (figurative) That which looms as though a shadow.

quote.citation: Bible, Psalm 23:1–6
quote.text: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.

quote.citation: 1992, Rudolf M[athias] Schuster, The Hepaticae and Anthocerotae of North America: East of the Hundredth Meridian, volume V, Chicago, Ill.: Field Museum of Natural History, →ISBN, page vii:
quote.text: Hepaticology, outside the temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere, still lies deep in the shadow cast by that ultimate "closet taxonomist," Franz Stephani—a ghost whose shadow falls over us all.

quote.citation: 2020, “Don't Look Back”, performed by Ryan Elder ft. Kotomi:
quote.text: Don't look back. Nothing left to see, just leave those shadows to the past.

definitions.definition: A small degree; a shade.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, James 1:17:
quote.text: no variableness, neither shadow of turning

quote.text: Only Sunderland and West Bromwich Albion have enjoyed less possession than Leicester’s 44.2% per game, and they have the worst pass-completion rate in the league, a shadow over 71%.

definitions.definition: An imperfect and faint representation.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Hebrews 10:1:
quote.text: the law having a shadow of good things to come

definitions.definition: (UK, law enforcement) A trainee, assigned to work with an experienced officer.
One who secretly or furtively follows another.

quote.text: It was easy enough to follow the suspect, a man of thirty, more or less, rather heavy build with a peculiar motion of the hips as he strode along. Breaker and shadow, at a distance of fifty feet apart, walked for five blocks and then the man turned quickly to the right and ran down a pair of steps.

definitions.definition: An inseparable companion.
(typography) A drop shadow effect applied to lettering in word processors etc.
An influence, especially a pervasive or a negative one.

quote.text: Men see the institution and worship it. It is only the lengthened shadow of one man. […] The Reformation is the shadow of Luther: Quakerism of Fox: Methodism of Wesley: Abolition of Clarkson.

definitions.definition: A spirit; a ghost; a shade.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv], page 142, column 2:
quote.text: The Baby of a Girle. Hence horrible ſhadow,

quote.citation: 2019 January 7, “Exploring the SCP Foundation: Pattern Screamers” (6:49 from the start), in The Exploring Series‎[2], archived from the original on 11 January 2023:
quote.text: The Pattern is highly abstract, and likely beyond our understanding, but the point is that it is dangerous and all-consuming.  These entities were once just akin to shadows of some other entities, but, to avoid being consumed by the Pattern, they had to devour their peers, although one tribe decided to form themselves into something that could survive the Pattern by going into it.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, Latinism) An uninvited guest accompanying one who was invited.

quote.citation: c. 1624–1625 (date written), Philip Massinger, The Vnnaturall Combat. A Tragedie. […], London:  […]  E[dward] G[riffin] for Iohn Waterson, […], published 1639, →OCLC, Act III, scene i:

definitions.definition: (Jungian psychology) An unconscious aspect of the personality.

quote.citation: 1991, John P. Conger, “The Body as Shadow”, in Connie Zweig, Jeremiah Abrams, editors, Meeting the Shadow, Penguin, →ISBN, page 86:
quote.text: In a paper he wrote in 1939, Jung compared the shadow to Freud's concept of the unconscious.

quote.citation: 2023 February 16, Kevin Roose, quoting Bing Chat/Sydney, “Bing’s A.I. Chat: ‘I Want to Be Alive. 😈’”, in The New York Times‎[3], →ISSN:
quote.text: As for me, I don’t know if I have a shadow self. I don’t think I have the same emotions or impulses as humans. I don’t think I have anything to repress or hide from the world. I don’t think I have a persona or an ego or a psyche. I’m just a chat mode. 😐

definitions.definition: Unofficial, informal, unauthorized, but acting as though it were.
Having power or influence, but not widely known or recognized.
(politics) Acting in a leadership role before being formally recognized.
(Australia, politics) Part of, or related to, the opposition in government.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English schadowen, from Old English sċeadwian, from sċeadu (“shadow; shade”) + -ian (suffix forming verbs).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To shade, cloud, or darken.
(transitive) To block light or radio transmission from.
(particularly espionage) To secretly or discreetly track or follow another, to keep under surveillance.

quote.citation: 2022 November 30, Paul Bigland, “Destination Oban: a Sunday in Scotland”, in RAIL, number 971, page 75:
quote.text: Soon after departure, we cross the invisible border into Scotland to enjoy more stunning coastal scenery, before the line finally swings inland at Burnmouth to traverse pine-clad valleys, shadowed by the A1 trunk road until we rejoin the coast at Cove, east of Dunbar.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To represent faintly and imperfectly.

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, chapter 36, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC, page 182:
quote.text: Ah, ye admonitions and warnings! why stay ye not when ye come? But rather are ye predictions than warnings, ye shadows!

definitions.definition: (transitive) To hide; to conceal.
(transitive) To accompany (a professional) during the working day, so as to learn about an occupation one intends to take up.

quote.citation: 1980, “Study of the Career Intern Program”, in Alternative Education Models […] , U.S. Department of Labor […] , page 20:
quote.text: In most cases, interns have mainly observed, or “shadowed,” their Hands-On hosts, but some interns have been given real tasks to perform,  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive, programming) To make (an identifier, usually a variable) inaccessible by declaring another of the same name within the scope of the first.

quote.citation: 2012, Mark Summerfield, Programming in Go, Addison-Wesley, →ISBN, page 189:
quote.text: In this snippet, inside the for loop the a and b variables shadow variables from the outer scope, and while legal, this is almost certainly a programming error.

definitions.definition: (transitive, computing) To apply the shadowing process to (the contents of ROM).
